strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important evaluation gap: long-form, multi-event text-to-video generation is not well served by benchmarks designed for short, single-scene clips.

Scope: The benchmark contains 240 prompts across 18 themes, derived from 30–60-second real videos, and evaluates nine diverse open-source systems. The reported 26 sub-dimensions cover visual quality, prompt adherence, temporal behavior, content clarity, and higher-level narrative properties.

Originality: Event-level alignment, separate intra-/inter-event consistency, and the attempt to evaluate narrative and thematic realization are useful directions beyond conventional FVD-, CLIP-, or frame-quality-based evaluation.

Presentation: The paper has a coherent high-level organization, provides the principal prompts and several metric formulations in the appendix, and reports detailed per-model and per-category results rather than only a single aggregate ranking.

Ethics: The authors explicitly discuss content filtering, personally identifiable information, harmful material, and copyright. Although the safeguards need substantiation, acknowledging these issues is valuable.
weaknesses: Soundness—missing validation: The central automatic metrics are never validated against human judgments. There is no human correlation study, inter-rater agreement, error analysis, or comparison with established evaluators for event alignment, content clarity, transition smoothness, or HERD. Consequently, the model rankings and the claim that the framework is “comprehensive and reliable” are not adequately supported.

Construct validity: HERD is called a Human Expectation Realization Degree, but both its targets and judgments are generated by language or vision-language models from a reference YouTube video; no humans provide expectations or evaluations. It therefore measures agreement with model-generated interpretations of one reference video, not demonstrated human satisfaction. Ignoring “unclear” answers in the denominator can also reward selective evaluator abstention.

Metric defects and underspecification: Event-level alignment averages only matched event pairs, so omitted ground-truth events are not penalized; its inversion term is undefined when fewer than two events are matched. The transition metric leaves k, feature weights, scaling constants, normalization, zero-transition behavior, and the treatment of MAE as a similarity unspecified. The embedding model for alignment, visual encoder for consistency, MLLMs used for several judgments, number of repeated trials, and sampling settings are also absent.

Experimental comparability: The paper does not report standardized output duration, resolution, frame rate, seeds, number of generations, decoding settings, or compute for the nine baselines. Some systems receive LLM-produced event prompts whereas others apparently receive the long original prompt, and the selected methods range from single-stream extension models to multi-shot agent pipelines. Without a precise protocol, performance differences cannot be confidently attributed to model capability.

Unsupported analysis: Similar scores across three broad content groups do not establish robustness. Low pairwise correlations do not establish absence of metric entanglement or bias, especially when samples from models and prompts are pooled. No confidence intervals, significance tests, hierarchical analysis, or sensitivity analysis to evaluator choice and stochasticity is presented. Several causal explanations in Sections 4.2–4.5 are therefore speculative.

Reproducibility: The release URL in the reproducibility statement is blank, the promised full code is deferred until after reorganization, and the stated initial JSON prompt suite is not part of the manuscript. Critical implementation constants, checkpoints, APIs, failure handling, and sample-level outputs are unavailable. The benchmark cannot currently be independently reproduced.

Dataset validity and ethics: The claim that downloading thousands of YouTube videos with yt-dlp complies with platform terms and copyright is asserted without license analysis. The paper does not document uploader consent, licenses, demographic representation, identifiable-person handling, or whether source videos will be redistributed. Manual filtering procedures and annotator protocol are also unspecified.

Presentation and limitations: Important notation and procedures are ambiguous, “TQ” is used for both technical and temporal quality, the content-clarity prompt is mislabeled as HERD, and several figures and tables are difficult to read. There is no substantive limitations section discussing evaluator bias, reference-video dependence, cultural subjectivity of narrative judgments, benchmark contamination, or computational cost. These issues compound the more decisive evidential weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Evaluating long-form video generation under complex, multi-event prompts is timely and potentially useful; the 240 prompts spanning 18 themes address a setting that short-video benchmarks cover poorly.

Scope: The evaluation includes nine open-source systems representing several long-video generation paradigms and reports results across static quality, alignment, temporal quality, content clarity, and higher-level narrative attributes.

Originality: Event-level alignment, intra- versus inter-event consistency, and the attempt to measure narrative or thematic realization offer useful extensions beyond conventional frame-quality and CLIP-based evaluation.
Presentation: The paper provides formulas, prompt templates, per-submetric tables, theme-stratified results, and qualitative examples, making the intended pipeline relatively easy to follow.
weaknesses: Soundness—central issue: The proposed metrics are never validated against human judgments. There are no human-rating protocols, agreement statistics, metric-human correlations, pairwise-ranking tests, or comparisons with established metrics. Consequently, the results do not establish that content clarity, HERD, event alignment, or transition smoothness measure their stated constructs. This is a critical deficiency for a benchmark paper.

HERD is described as measuring human expectations, but its targets are generated by Seed1.5-VL/Qwen2.5-VL from source videos, converted into questions by DeepSeek, and answered by another MLLM. No humans define or verify these expectations. The name and the paper's conclusions therefore overstate what is measured.

HERD discards every "unclear" response from its denominator, creating selective-abstention bias and potentially undefined or inflated scores when the evaluator is uncertain. Neither the rate of unclear answers nor handling of an all-unclear case is reported.

The event-alignment formulation averages only over matched event pairs and apparently does not penalize unmatched ground-truth events or spurious generated events. A video containing one accurately matched event while omitting most requested events could therefore score highly. The inversion normalization is also undefined for fewer than two matches, and no edge-case policy is specified.

Several new metrics are materially underspecified. The paper does not identify the embedding model used for semantic similarities, the MLLMs used for several evaluations, similarity normalization, matching thresholds, the number of repeated trials R, or key transition-metric constants and weights. It also does not explain failure handling for event grounding, segmentation, scene detection, or absent subjects.

Transition smoothness is not convincingly defined: abrupt cinematic cuts are not necessarily defects, while PySceneDetect preferentially finds discontinuities. The variance-based formula, its normalization, and its use of MAE as a "similarity" lack justification, ablations, or human validation.

The benchmark construction risks circularity and source-model bias: MLLMs describe real videos, other LLMs extract events and judgments from those descriptions, and related MLLMs then evaluate generated videos. The study does not test sensitivity to evaluator choice, prompt wording, decoding randomness, or model-family bias.

Baseline comparability is unclear. Some methods receive LLM-generated event-level prompts while others apparently receive different input representations; output duration, resolution, frame rate, random seeds, number of generations, checkpoint choices, and generation budgets are not systematically controlled or reported. This weakens model rankings.

The empirical analyses do not support their stated conclusions. Small differences across content categories are called evidence of robustness without uncertainty estimates or hypothesis tests. Correlations pool samples from multiple generators, apparently treating dependent outputs from the same prompts as independent, and low pairwise correlation does not demonstrate absence of metric entanglement or bias.

The paper reports no confidence intervals, variance across generation seeds or judge calls, statistical significance tests, test-retest reliability, or sensitivity analyses. Given stochastic generators and MLLM judges, point estimates to two decimal places convey unjustified precision.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the release URL in the reproducibility statement is blank, the complete code is deferred until after reorganization, and the paper omits hardware, inference cost, seeds, exact model/checkpoint versions, and many hyperparameters. Others could not presently reproduce the reported rankings.

Presentation needs substantial polishing. Terminology and acronyms collide (TQ denotes both technical quality and temporal quality), some prompt headings are mislabeled, placeholder few-shot examples remain, and numerous grammatical and typesetting issues reduce clarity. The paper also claims prompts are "evenly distributed" over 18 themes although 240 cannot be divided evenly among them.

Originality is incremental relative to VBench/VBench-Long, VBench 2.0, EvalCrafter, and other recent video benchmarks. The new high-level dimensions could differentiate the work, but without construct validation they remain proposed automated proxies rather than established benchmark measures.

The ethical statement is too conclusory. Downloading YouTube videos with yt-dlp is asserted to comply with terms and copyright without discussing licenses, creator consent, redistribution rights, jurisdiction, or whether videos themselves will be released. Filtering criteria and annotator procedures are also undocumented.

No substantive limitations section acknowledges evaluator hallucination, demographic or cultural subjectivity in emotional and thematic judgments, dependence on proprietary/API models, dataset-source bias, metric gaming, or copyright constraints. These omissions matter because the benchmark makes broad claims about human expectations.

strengths: Significance: The paper targets the timely and practically important problem of evaluating long-form text-to-video generation under complex, multi-event prompts.

Originality: LoCoT2V-Bench combines 240 real-video-derived prompts across 18 themes with event-level alignment, intra-/inter-event consistency, content clarity, and the proposed HERD dimensions; this is broader than conventional short-video quality benchmarks.

Empirical breadth: Nine open-source systems spanning diffusion, autoregressive, and multi-stage generation paradigms are evaluated using 26 sub-dimensions. The resulting tables expose potentially useful weaknesses in event alignment, cross-event consistency, and narrative realization.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, provides formulas and evaluation prompts in the appendix, and includes aggregate, theme-level, correlation, and qualitative results. The rendered figures and tables are legible overall. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d440351ba9f84aa4ae4f052cf69861a1/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that the benchmark is reliable is unsupported by human validation. No human ratings, inter-rater agreement, metric-human correlations, or comparison against established metrics is reported. This is especially serious for subjective constructs such as emotional response, narrative flow, themes, interpretive depth, and overall impression, despite the name Human Expectation Realization Degree.

The event-alignment formulation appears not to penalize missing ground-truth events adequately: it averages over the matched pairs, with N defined as the number of matches. A video containing only a small subset of accurately rendered events could therefore score well. Edge cases such as zero or one matched event, for which the inversion normalization can be undefined, are not specified.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Small differences across three broad theme groups are treated as proof of robustness, while low correlations are used to claim that biases or metric entanglement are controlled. No confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, sensitivity analyses, evaluator-model ablations, or uncertainty from repeated generations are provided; Table 5 also does not clearly identify the three selected methods or justify pooling their samples.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate. The code and complete benchmark are only promised after acceptance, and essential settings are missing, including generation seeds and sampling protocols, output duration/FPS/resolution, number of generations per prompt, evaluator decoding settings and repetition count, embedding model, normalization choices, and transition-score hyperparameters. Exact baseline adaptations are particularly important because some methods require different input formats.

The metric construction contains unresolved validity concerns. HERD targets and questions are generated from MLLM assessments of source videos and then judged by another MLLM, creating model-dependent and potentially circular supervision. Excluding 'unclear' answers from the HERD denominator can bias scores upward, and no unclear-response rates are reported. Similarly, treating gradual transitions as preferable does not account for intentional cinematic hard cuts.

Ethics and limitations are insufficiently treated. The assertion that downloading thousands of YouTube videos with yt-dlp complies with terms and copyright law is not substantiated; licenses, creator consent, geographic legal basis, storage, and redistribution plans are unspecified. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering demographic/cultural bias in themes and evaluators, dependence on proprietary LLMs, evaluator contamination, and benchmark gaming. These weaknesses prevent reliable use of the proposed benchmark despite its promising scope.

strengths: Significance: The paper targets an important and under-evaluated setting—long, multi-scene video generation from complex prompts—and provides a useful suite of 234 prompts spanning 18 themes, averaging six scenes and 248.85 words.

Originality: The hierarchical scene/character/background/camera metadata and gated, scene-wise fine-grained alignment evaluation offer a more diagnostic treatment of prompt adherence than a single global score. HERD is also a promising attempt to assess narrative and affective properties.

Evaluation breadth: Thirteen diverse generation pipelines are evaluated across perceptual, alignment, temporal, dynamic, and expectation-realization dimensions. Tables 2, 4–6 and the category-level analyses provide substantial empirical coverage.

Soundness strengths: The authors validate automatic metrics against judgments from three annotators, report PLCC, SRCC, and KRCC, keep the 100-video dynamic-quality fitting set disjoint from the human-alignment set, and compare HERD against two alternative implementations.

Presentation: The main narrative is generally clear, the appendix includes prompts and implementation descriptions, and the paper openly notes weaknesses such as possible auditor hallucination and imbalanced category sizes.
weaknesses: Soundness: The human validation is too limited to establish the claimed reliability. Only 5% of generated videos are annotated, with no exact sample count, sampling stratification, confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-annotator agreement, or annotator training/demographics. Several reported correlations are only moderate (e.g., character consistency SRCC 0.499 and multiple HERD subdimensions near 0.41–0.48), yet the paper concludes broadly that the framework aligns well with human judgment.

The baseline comparison is insufficiently controlled. Results use only one generation seed, so no uncertainty or run-to-run variability is reported. Output duration and frame-count policies are not specified, and several models use default/recommended resolution settings instead of the nominal 480p setting. These differences can directly affect perceptual, temporal, and dynamic metrics and weaken the method rankings.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The central video-understanding MLLM used for overall alignment, fine-grained VQA, character verification, and HERD is repeatedly described only as a 'strong MLLM.' Model/version, decoding settings, frame sampling, and repetition protocol are absent. Likewise, the PQ scale parameters and sampling ratios, warping-error normalization constant, fitted dynamic-quality coefficients, and many thresholds are not provided, and there is no clear code/data release statement.

Some dynamic-quality definitions are technically unclear or apparently inconsistent. In Eq. 8, a video divided into segments of length rN is indexed as having floor(rN) segment features, and a double sum over pairs is normalized by only floor(rN), so the expression is not evidently bounded or dimensionally consistent. Temporal entropy is merely said to be estimated with FFmpeg, without an operational definition. These problems matter because the fitted aggregate DQ is used in the main conclusions.

HERD remains partly circular and weakly grounded: GPT-5 infers subjective expectations from the prompt, another unspecified MLLM judges fulfillment, and only a small human sample validates the result. The alternative baselines reuse the same evaluator, so they do not test robustness across judge models or prompt formulations. No comparison to direct human assessment reliability or established narrative-quality instruments is given.

The prompt suite is derived from curated, relatively high-quality YouTube videos and then expanded into story-like prompts by GPT-5. This may favor professionally structured content and LLM-like language rather than representative user requests. The manuscript does not test generalization to naturally authored prompts or report detailed coverage within the 18 themes.

Presentation is occasionally difficult: Figures 1–2 are extremely dense at page scale, and essential implementation choices are dispersed across a long appendix. The term OA is also overloaded between 'Overall Alignment' and the conference's overall assessment terminology.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. There is no dedicated limitations discussion covering evaluator-model dependence, stochastic uncertainty, benchmark contamination, demographic/cultural subjectivity of HERD, or source-domain bias. The impact statement asserts compliance with YouTube terms and copyright regulations but does not explain licensing or redistribution rights, consent/privacy treatment for depicted people, dataset takedown procedures, or annotator compensation and welfare. These unresolved issues reduce confidence that others can safely build on or redistribute the benchmark.

strengths: Significance: Long-form, multi-scene text-to-video evaluation is timely, and the suite covers 234 prompts across 18 themes and 13 generation methods. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/9d62e74788af46baa4883ed88171e4bb/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Originality: The hierarchical scene/character/background/camera metadata, gated fine-grained VQA, character-consistency pipeline, and HERD framework form a broader diagnostic suite than standard short-video benchmarks.

Soundness: The authors attempt human validation rather than relying exclusively on automatic metrics; three annotators assess 5% of generated videos, and PLCC, SRCC, and KRCC are reported for many subdimensions.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. The overview, main comparison table, prompts, baseline descriptions, and qualitative samples make the intended pipeline understandable.
The paper reports detailed per-method and category-level results, exposing potentially useful failure patterns such as weak fine-grained alignment and character consistency.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several metric definitions are incomplete or mathematically questionable. Equation 8 sums similarities over all j≠i but divides only by the number of segments, so the stated global-aperiodicity score can become negative. Equation 9 is a mean distance from the feature mean, not a variance. The multi-scale PQ equation does not clearly aggregate scales, and the warping-error normalization constant is unspecified. These defects directly affect central benchmark scores.

Soundness: Human validation is too weak to justify the claim that the framework is effective. Correlations are often only about 0.4–0.55, character consistency has SRCC 0.499, and no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, inter-annotator agreement, annotator blinding, or per-model/per-prompt analysis is provided. Pooling all samples may inflate correlations through between-model differences.

The scene-wise FGA procedure does not establish reliable temporal localization: a scene-existence question gates subsequent questions, but the manuscript does not explain how the relevant interval is isolated. The sequential character anchoring is order-dependent, while equal averaging across attributes, actions, facets, and scenes is not validated. No robustness study examines question order, MLLM stochasticity, evaluator choice, or gating errors.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The central video evaluator and verifier are repeatedly called only a 'strong MLLM'; their identity, decoding settings, sampling protocol, and versions are absent. Key metadata/question-generation procedures are insufficiently specified, and no code or dataset release commitment is given. Proprietary GPT-5 is also embedded in construction and HERD evaluation.

Important implementation parameters are missing, including PQ scale and sampling values, the warping normalization coefficient, dynamic-quality regression coefficients/intercept and preprocessing, generated video durations/frame counts, failure handling, and many baseline-specific settings. Thus the reported rankings cannot be independently reconstructed.

The baseline comparison is not controlled sufficiently. Only one generation seed is used; some methods use 480p while others use default settings; input interfaces differ; and StoryAdapter is augmented with Wan2.2, introducing another generator. Output duration is not standardized or even reported, despite duration being central to long-form evaluation. There are no uncertainty estimates or significance tests for rankings.

The very high background-consistency and warping scores do not convincingly demonstrate long-term temporal quality. Adjacent-frame full-image similarity is confounded by static content, character appearance, and camera motion, while warping error is also local. The authors' own correlations with human background judgments are only moderate, yet the conclusions characterize temporal stability as robust or exceptional.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: many components are adaptations or combinations of DeQA, VBench, EvalCrafter, DEVIL, SAM, CLIP, RAFT, and MLLM judging. HERD is potentially useful, but its six dimensions overlap, and its validation is limited to comparisons against two closely related MLLM prompting strategies.

The complexity comparison is based on a single LLM's subjective 1–10 ratings, without human validation or sensitivity to the judge. Prompt length and automatically added detail may produce high scores without establishing greater diagnostic difficulty; the reported complexity-performance correlations are near zero.

Dataset construction may reduce ecological validity: prompts originate from real videos but are expanded with invented names, traits, and story elements. The manuscript provides little evidence that the final prompts remain fully grounded, diverse, or representative beyond aggregate counts and LLM-derived complexity scores.

Limitations and ethics are treated inadequately. There is no substantive limitations section discussing evaluator bias, benchmark contamination, language/cultural coverage, proprietary-model dependence, or metric gaming. The ethics statement asserts that YouTube collection complies with copyright and platform rules but gives no license filtering, creator consent, redistribution policy, or data-governance details; annotator recruitment and compensation are also unspecified.

Presentation is readable, but some central methodological details are replaced by vague language such as 'strong MLLM' and 'empirically set,' while extensive appendix space is spent reproducing prompts and baseline summaries. Given that unsupported metric outputs drive every main conclusion, these omissions prevent acceptance despite the useful benchmark direction.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important and timely gap—evaluation of long-form, multi-scene text-to-video generation—and the benchmark could be useful to both model developers and evaluators.

Scope: LoCoT2V-Bench contains 234 prompts averaging 248.85 words and six scenes, with hierarchical character, background, action, and camera metadata. Evaluating 13 diverse methods produces a comparatively broad empirical snapshot of the field.

Originality: The scene-gated hierarchical VQA evaluation, explicit character-consistency pipeline, streaming adaptations for long videos, and HERD formulation collectively go beyond simply applying existing short-video metrics.

Evidence: The main results expose informative capability differences, particularly the contrast between high background-consistency scores and much lower character consistency, and between overall and fine-grained prompt alignment.

Validation effort: The authors obtain judgments from three annotators on a 5% sample, report PLCC, SRCC, and KRCC, compare alternative HERD implementations, and test the effect of character masking on background consistency.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, visually clear, and unusually detailed in its appendix, including prompt templates, metric definitions, baseline settings, dataset statistics, and category-level results.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several central automatic metrics remain only moderately validated. Fine-grained alignment has SRCC 0.527, character consistency 0.499, and most HERD subdimensions approximately 0.41–0.48. Nevertheless, the paper sometimes describes these results as confirming effectiveness or robustness without uncertainty estimates or comparisons against established evaluators.

Reproducibility: The central video-scoring MLLM is repeatedly described only as a “strong MLLM”; its identity, version, decoding configuration, and evaluation cost are not specified. There is also no concrete code, data, generated-video, or cached-score release commitment. Dependence on GPT-5 and other changing proprietary services further limits exact reproduction.

Human evaluation is underspecified: The paper provides no inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, annotator recruitment or compensation information, or detailed training protocol. Treating the approximately 5% sample as independent also ignores clustering by prompt and generation method.

Metric construction needs stronger justification. Major scores are formed by equal averaging of heterogeneous submetrics with different semantics and calibration. Dynamic Quality uses a linear model fitted on only 100 annotated videos, but the coefficients, normalization, held-out performance, and cross-validation are absent. Some mathematical definitions are ambiguous or appear improperly normalized, including the multi-scale PQ aggregation and global-aperiodicity sum.

The comparative experiment is not fully controlled: only one generation seed is used; several models run at different resolutions or recommended settings; multi-prompt methods receive LLM-derived scene decompositions; and StoryAdapter is augmented with Wan2.2 image-to-video generation. These choices may materially affect rankings, yet no sensitivity analysis is provided.

Some metrics do not cleanly measure their stated constructs. Background consistency is computed on complete frames and can therefore reward stable characters rather than backgrounds; character consistency conditions on successfully detected and verified instances, potentially overlooking missing characters; and the scene-existence gate can cause one fallible MLLM answer to zero every descendant alignment score.

The claimed complexity advantage is established using a single LLM judge, while the new prompts have very low complexity-score variance and complexity correlates only weakly with model performance. This makes the 8.70 complexity figure less persuasive as evidence of benchmark difficulty.

Ethics and limitations are inadequate. The impact statement asserts that downloading YouTube videos with yt-dlp complies with terms and copyright law but gives no licensing, creator-consent, redistribution, geographic, or takedown analysis. The paper also lacks a candid limitations section covering evaluator bias, proprietary-model dependence, cultural subjectivity in HERD, and benchmark contamination.

Overall, the benchmark is promising and potentially valuable, but the insufficient specification and validation of the central evaluators prevent reliable reproduction and make the method rankings less conclusive than required for acceptance in the current form.
